summary: 18 claims on the cost of workplace incidents and the return on prevention. 15 were checked on a fetched page or PDF. The 3 NSC figures could not be fetched (HTTP 403), so they are marked low and backed by two secondary pages. They cover ILO deaths, injuries and GDP share, the construction share of fatal accidents, US NSC unit costs, UK HSE per-case costs, three return-on-prevention figures (2.2, $2 or more, $4 to $6), Saudi injury rates and construction share, a Saudi wage anchor with weekly hours, and delay and overrun anchors. Main gaps: no Saudi or GCC cost of a fatality, no construction-only wage, no labour share of project cost.

claims.topic: ILO global estimate: work-related deaths and non-fatal injuries per year
claims.figure: around 2.93 million workers died from work-related factors; over 395 million workers sustained a non-fatal work injury
claims.measures: Status: stat. ILO estimates covering the year 2019. Of the 2.93 million deaths, 2.6 million came from work-related diseases and 330,000 from work accidents (same page). Deaths are up more than 12 per cent on 2000 and equal 6.71 per cent of all deaths globally (same page). Location: PDF page 4, section 'Where are we now?'. The ILO news release of 26 Nov 2023 repeats 'nearly three million' deaths and 395 million non-fatal injuries (https://www.ilo.org/resource/news/nearly-3-million-people-die-work-related-accidents-and-diseases). A later ILO paper (Oct 2025, p.8) repeats 2.93 million for 2019. I read the PDF by downloading it and extracting its text locally.
claims.source_title: A call for safer and healthier working environments
claims.quote: over 395 million workers worldwide sustained a non-fatal work injury. In addition, around 2.93 million workers died as a result of work-related factors
claims.use_in_story: Open the cost chapter with one counter that climbs to 2.93 million deaths and 395 million injuries, then zoom down to a single construction site.

claims.topic: ILO headline: share of world GDP lost to work-related injuries and illness
claims.figure: 3.94 per cent of global GDP per year, or 2.99 trillion US dollars
claims.measures: Status: stat. Cost of work-related illnesses and injuries as announced by the ILO on 4 September 2017. The page does not state the data year behind the estimate. This is the older and most quoted ILO share. The same page gives 2.78 million work-related deaths a year, which the ILO's 2023 report has since replaced with 2.93 million. Newer estimates are in the next claim.
claims.year: 2017 (published 4 Sep 2017; data year not stated on the page)
claims.source_title: ILO head calls for global coalition on safety and health at work
claims.quote: represent 3.94 per cent of global GDP per year, or 2.99 trillion US dollars
claims.use_in_story: Show a world economy disc with a 3.94 per cent slice peeling away, labelled 2.99 trillion US dollars a year.

claims.topic: Newer estimate: work-related harm as a share of global GDP
claims.figure: around 5 percent of global GDP (ILO paper, Oct 2025); 5.8% of global GDP (peer-reviewed paper, 2019 data)
claims.measures: Status: stat. ILO issue paper of October 2025, p.5: work-related harm 'imposes significant economic losses, estimated at around 5 percent of global GDP'. On p.27 the same paper says earlier estimates showed losses 'exceeding 3%' and that 'the cost now exceeds 4% of GDP'. Both cite a 2024 peer-reviewed paper (Scandinavian Journal of Work, Environment & Health 2024;50(2):73-82) whose abstract, fetched at https://www.sjweh.fi/article/4132, prints 'an associated economic loss of 5.8% of global GDP', with 2.9 million work-attributed deaths in 2019 (2.58 million from disease, 0.32 million from injuries) and 180 million DALYs. The same paper's main-text Results gives the loss as '6% of the global GDP' (https://www.sjweh.fi/show_abstract.php?abstract_id=4132&fullText=1). The ILO figures differ by page and from the 2017 headline, so a slide should say 'more than 4 per cent' or 'about 4 to 6 per cent' and name the source. I read the ILO PDF by downloading it and extracting its text locally.
claims.source_title: Issue Paper: OSH Statistics. Supporting the review and update of the international OSH statistical standards at the 22nd ICLS in 2028
claims.quote: Work-related harm also imposes significant economic losses, estimated at around 5 percent of global GDP
claims.use_in_story: Step the GDP slice up from 3.94 per cent to around 5 per cent to show that newer estimates are higher than the classic ILO number.

claims.topic: ILO: construction share of fatal work accidents
claims.figure: one in six fatal accidents at work occur on a construction site; no less than 60,000 fatal accidents a year
claims.measures: Status: stat. ILO figures quoted at an ILO and IIRSM forum, in an ILO news item dated 12 Oct 2017. The data year is not stated and the count is a floor ('no less than'). Newer ILO context, 2023 report, PDF page 8 (https://www.ilo.org/media/358981/download): agriculture, forestry and fishing, mining, construction and manufacturing together see 200,000 fatal injuries a year, 60 per cent of all fatal occupational injuries, and 'the mining and quarrying, construction, and utilities sectors are the three most hazardous sectors globally' by fatal injury rate. I did not find a newer ILO construction-only count.
claims.year: 2017 (published); the ranking is from the 2023 report
claims.source_title: ILO and IIRSM social dialogue on occupational health and safety calls for improved safety in the construction industry
claims.quote: one in six fatal accidents at work occur on a construction site globally, no less than 60,000 fatal accidents occur on construction sites
claims.use_in_story: Draw six site icons, light one in red, then run a counter toward 60,000 a year.

claims.topic: US National Safety Council: cost of one work-related death
claims.measures: Status: stat. Societal economic cost per work-related death in the US, as NSC Injury Facts 'Work Injury Costs' reports it for 2024. The secondary page says it leaves out lost quality of life. The NSC Injury Facts site returned HTTP 403 to every automated fetch I tried (seven pages), and the one NSC webinar PDF I could open shows its work-cost slide as an image only, so I could not read this page. The figure was read in search-engine extracts of the NSC page and matches two fetched secondary pages: https://reliamag.com/guides/cost-of-a-workplace-injury/ and https://www.eznewswire.com/newsroom/armstrong-lee-baker-workplace-injury-cost-estimates (a press release dated 31 Aug 2026). Open the NSC URL in a normal browser to confirm. Latest year seen is 2024; a 2025 update may follow.
claims.quote: Not from the NSC page. Secondary page (reliamag.com guide) says: 'A death cost about $1.54 million, per the National Safety Council'
claims.use_in_story: Run a counter up to $1.54 million for one life lost, then set it beside the $48,000 injury cost so the gap is plain.

claims.topic: US National Safety Council: cost of one medically consulted work injury
claims.measures: Status: stat. Societal economic cost per medically consulted work injury in the US for 2024, as NSC labels it. It is a cost to society (wages, medical, administration), not a single employer's bill. The NSC Injury Facts site returned HTTP 403 to every automated fetch I tried (seven pages), and the one NSC webinar PDF I could open shows its work-cost slide as an image only, so I could not read this page. The figure was read in search-engine extracts of the NSC page and matches two fetched secondary pages: https://reliamag.com/guides/cost-of-a-workplace-injury/ and https://www.eznewswire.com/newsroom/armstrong-lee-baker-workplace-injury-cost-estimates (a press release dated 31 Aug 2026). Open the NSC URL in a normal browser to confirm. Latest year seen is 2024; a 2025 update may follow.
claims.quote: Not from the NSC page. Secondary page (reliamag.com guide) says: 'A medically consulted injury cost about $48,000 in 2024'
claims.use_in_story: Pop a $48,000 price tag on each injury icon so a viewer sees what one prevented injury is worth.

claims.topic: US National Safety Council: total yearly cost of work injuries
claims.figure: $181.4 billion total cost of work injuries (2024)
claims.measures: Status: stat. National total for 2024. The press release and the NSC extracts give $54.9 billion wage and productivity losses, $36.8 billion medical and $64.5 billion administrative costs inside it. The press release also reports 102 million lost days in 2024. The secondary guide warns that NSC's cost per worker ($1,120 in 2024) must not be read as the cost of one injury. The NSC Injury Facts site returned HTTP 403 to every automated fetch I tried (seven pages), and the one NSC webinar PDF I could open shows its work-cost slide as an image only, so I could not read this page. The figure was read in search-engine extracts of the NSC page and matches two fetched secondary pages: https://reliamag.com/guides/cost-of-a-workplace-injury/ and https://www.eznewswire.com/newsroom/armstrong-lee-baker-workplace-injury-cost-estimates (a press release dated 31 Aug 2026). Open the NSC URL in a normal browser to confirm. Latest year seen is 2024; a 2025 update may follow.
claims.quote: Not from the NSC page. Press release (fetched, 31 Aug 2026) says: 'work injuries cost the United States $181.4 billion in 2024'
claims.use_in_story: Grow a US bar to $181.4 billion next to the UK bar of £22.9bn to show that rich countries still pay a large yearly bill.

claims.topic: UK HSE: yearly cost of work-related injury and ill health, and cost per case
claims.figure: £22.9bn in 2023/24; £10,000 per case (injury); £24,200 per case (ill health)
claims.measures: Status: stat. Great Britain, 2023 prices. Same page splits the total into £6.5bn from injuries and £16.4bn from ill health, and into £13.4bn for individuals, £4.3bn for employers and £5.2bn for government. 'Per case' is HSE's equivalent unit cost. The page header showed an update date of 2026-01-15 in my fetch. I fetched the page twice and the figures matched.
claims.source_title: Costs to Great Britain of workplace injuries and new cases of work-related ill health - 2023 to 2024
claims.quote: Total Costs to Britain were around £22.9bn in 2023/24 ... equivalent to unit cost of £10,000 per case ... equivalent to unit cost of £24,200 per case
claims.use_in_story: Show two price tags, £10,000 for an injury and £24,200 for an ill-health case, then a yearly total bar of £22.9bn.

claims.topic: ISSA: return on prevention of company safety and health spending
claims.figure: Return on Prevention 2.2 (prevention benefit divided by prevention cost)
claims.measures: Status: stat. International study run by ISSA with the German social accident insurance bodies, completed 12/2012 per the DGUV project page. The same page says 75% of interviewed companies expect extra safety and health spending to leave costs the same or lower over the long term, and gives an earlier German ratio of 1.6 (2006 to 2008). The ISSA PDF at issa.int returned HTTP 403, so I could not confirm the number of companies and countries. This is a company-level average across sectors, not a construction figure.
claims.source_title: Return on Prevention - ISSA (research project page)
claims.publisher: DGUV, Institute for Work and Health (IAG), for the International Social Security Association (ISSA)
claims.quote: The Return on Prevention (ROP) is assessed 2.2.
claims.use_in_story: Draw a balance scale with 1 unit of prevention spend on one side and 2.2 units coming back on the other.

claims.topic: OSHA business case: what finance chiefs say prevention returns
claims.figure: each $1 invested in injury prevention returns $2 or more (over 60 percent of CFOs in the survey)
claims.measures: Status: stat. A survey statement hosted on OSHA's Business Case page. The page credits a Liberty Mutual Insurance Company Chief Financial Officer Survey of 2005. It is what executives say, not a measured return. The same page says employers paid more than $1 billion per week in direct workers' compensation costs for disabling, non-fatal workplace injuries, citing the Liberty Mutual 2025 Workplace Safety Index.
claims.source_title: Business Case for Safety and Health - Overview
claims.publisher: US Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
claims.quote: Over 60 percent of chief financial officers in one survey reported that each $1 invested in injury prevention returns $2 or more.
claims.use_in_story: Flip a coin that lands as $1 in and $2 or more out, labelled 'what finance chiefs say'.

claims.topic: OSHA regulatory analysis quoted by ASSP: return on effective safety programs
claims.figure: a return of $4 to $6 for every $1 invested, with injury and illness rates down 20% or greater
claims.measures: Status: stat. The ASSP white paper (2020 version, PDF page 8) quotes OSHA's Office of Regulatory Analysis. The paper gives no year or document for the OSHA statement, so treat this as an older, upper-end figure. The sentence did not appear in my fetch of OSHA's own Business Case page. The same page of the paper lists a 2001 Liberty Mutual survey in which 61 percent of executives said $3 or more is saved for each $1. I read the PDF by downloading it and extracting its text locally.
claims.year: Not stated (older OSHA statement; paper is the 2020 version)
claims.source_title: The Return on Investment for Safety, Health, and Environmental (OSH) Management Programs
claims.publisher: American Society of Safety Professionals (ASSP), Council on Practices and Standards
claims.quote: a return of $4 to $6 for every $1 invested
claims.use_in_story: Show a return range running from 2.2 (ISSA) up to 4 to 6 (OSHA analysis) so the slide says 'at least double, often more'.

claims.topic: Saudi Arabia: occupational injury rate per 100 thousand workers
claims.figure: 245.7 non-fatal and 1.1 fatal occupational injuries per 100 thousand workers
claims.measures: Status: stat. Workers aged 15 and over, excluding road traffic accidents. The disclaimer says the injury rate comes from register data of the National Council for Occupational Safety and Health. A chart in the same PDF also lists 280.4 and 3.1 for 'All work injuries'. I read those as the rates when transport injuries are included, but chart labels are not a sentence, so treat that reading as unconfirmed. Not split by sector. Location: page 1, Figure 1. I read the PDF by downloading it and extracting its text locally.
claims.source_title: Health and Safety at Workplace Statistics 2024
claims.quote: rate of non-fatal occupational injuries was 245.7, while the rate of fatal occupational injuries was 1.1 per 100 thousand workers
claims.use_in_story: Use 1.1 deaths per 100 thousand workers as the Saudi baseline and tick 245.7 injuries beside it.

claims.topic: GOSI: change in registered work injuries in 2023
claims.measures: Status: stat. General Organization for Social Insurance (GOSI) statistics as reported by the Saudi Press Agency. Only the headline came through my fetch, because the article body did not load, so the absolute injury count and the cause split are not confirmed here. The Arabic version of the page (https://spa.gov.sa/N2073302) gave the same headline only. The peer-reviewed GOSI analysis in the next claim also shows a falling trend for 2016 to 2021.
claims.source_title: GOSI: Work Injuries Decreased by 8.5% during 2023
claims.publisher: Saudi Press Agency (SPA), reporting GOSI statistics
claims.quote: GOSI: Work Injuries Decreased by 8.5% during 2023
claims.use_in_story: Show the Saudi injury line stepping down 8.5% in 2023 as a baseline that new tools should keep bending.

claims.topic: Saudi Arabia: construction share of GOSI-recorded work injuries, and deaths
claims.figure: construction was 42%-48% of all work injuries (2016 to 2021); 1,009 work-related deaths, averaging 168 per year
claims.measures: Status: stat. Peer-reviewed analysis of GOSI open data for insured workers, 2016 to 2021 (the paper's stated scope). The discussion gives construction as 45.1% of injuries in 2016 and 41.6% in 2021, down from 51% in 2015 cited from earlier work. The 1,009 deaths cover all sectors. The paper says injury rates fell by 31%-52% in all sectors between 2016 and 2021, except agriculture and fishing, which fell by only 5% in 2021. Published 6 March 2023, open access. I read the PDF by downloading it and extracting its text locally.
claims.source_title: The Epidemiology of Work-Related Injuries in Saudi Arabia Between 2016 and 2021
claims.quote: Injuries in the construction sector comprised 42%-48% of all injuries, followed by the commerce sector.
claims.use_in_story: Colour close to half of the injury icons in the Saudi tower as construction.

claims.topic: Saudi wage anchor: average monthly wage in Industry, which includes construction
claims.figure: 4,893 SAR per month for non-Saudi paid employees in Industry (5,606 SAR for all nationalities)
claims.measures: Status: stat. GASTAT labour market statistics for Q4 2025, republished by the Gulf Labour Markets, Migration and Population programme. GASTAT groups activities as Agriculture, Industry and Services. The page says Industry includes mining, manufacturing, electricity and gas supply, water supply, and construction, so this is a proxy and not a construction-only wage. For hours, GASTAT survey data hosted by KAPSARC give 47 average usual hours of main work per week for non-Saudis in Q2 2025, all sectors (https://datasource.kapsarc.org/api/explore/v2.1/catalog/datasets/labor-force-survey-data/records?where=indicator%3D%22Average%20Usual%20Hours%20of%20main%20Work%20for%20Employed%20Persons%20(Hours%2FWeek)%22&order_by=year%20desc%2C%20quarter%20desc&limit=12). The same dataset gives 4,695 SAR for Industry non-Saudis in Q2 2025. Derived arithmetic, not a published figure: 4,893 / (47 x 52 / 12) is about 24 SAR per hour. The 24 SAR is wage only and mixes two quarters.
claims.source_title: Saudi Arabia: Average monthly wages per paid employee in main employment by nationality (Saudi/non-Saudi), sex and aggregated category of economic activities (in SR) (Q4 2025)
claims.publisher: GLMM (Gulf Research Center), data from GASTAT Labour Market Statistics
claims.quote: Table row 'Industry', Non-Saudis group, Total column: 4,893; Total group, Total column: 5,606 (in SR). Source line: Labour Market Statistics, General Authority for Statistics
claims.use_in_story: Turn lost hours into riyals with a dial that reads about 24 SAR of wage per lost hour (derived), before any delay or claim cost.

claims.topic: Saudi Arabia: construction is the largest employer, plus the all-sector wage
claims.figure: 3,348,143 employees in Construction; average monthly wage 5.8 thousand SAR across all sectors
claims.measures: Status: stat. GASTAT labour market statistics for the second quarter of 2026, shown on the DataSaudi portal. Construction is the activity with the most employees. The 5.8 thousand SAR wage is per paid employee in main work across all sectors, so it is not a construction wage (the page prints it with the riyal sign). My fetch did not show whether the headcount is register-based or survey-based. The page also names wholesale and retail trade (1,803,668) and administrative and support services (1,526,099) as the next two.
claims.publisher: General Authority for Statistics (GASTAT), DataSaudi portal
claims.quote: the economic activities that registered the highest number of employees in Saudi Arabia were Construction (3,348,143 employees)
claims.use_in_story: Fill a map of the Kingdom with 3.35 million construction workers, the biggest workforce in the country, to show how many people are exposed.

claims.topic: Saudi project delays: how often large projects overrun time
claims.figure: 70% of projects experienced time overrun; average overrun between 10% and 30% of the original duration
claims.measures: Status: stat. Peer-reviewed survey of 23 contractors, 19 consultants and 15 owners on large building projects in Saudi Arabia. It found 73 causes of delay, and change orders were the most common. 76% of contractors and 56% of consultants said the average overrun is 10% to 30%. The abstract also says 45 out of 76 projects were delayed (59%), which differs from the 70% headline, so quote 70% as the survey's conclusion. The study is from 2006, so use it as a pattern, not a current rate. International Journal of Project Management 24(4), 349-357.
claims.source_title: Causes of delay in large construction projects
claims.publisher: International Journal of Project Management (peer-reviewed); record held by KFUPM
claims.quote: Surveys concluded that 70% of projects experienced time overrun
claims.use_in_story: Show a planned bar and an actual bar that runs 10 to 30 percent longer, stamped '7 in 10 projects'.

claims.topic: Megaproject overruns: how often giant projects finish over budget and late
claims.figure: nine out of ten megaprojects have cost overruns; about one in ten is on budget and one in ten on schedule
claims.measures: Status: stat. Peer-reviewed overview of megaproject performance data (Project Management Journal 45(2), 2014, pp. 6-19), read from the author's draft on arXiv. Overruns of up to 50 percent in real terms are common and over 50 percent not uncommon. It covers very large projects, so it fits giga-projects and not every site. The paper also puts global megaproject spending at USD 6-9 trillion a year, about 8 percent of world GDP. I read the PDF by downloading it and extracting its text locally.
claims.source_title: What You Should Know About Megaprojects, and Why: An Overview
claims.publisher: Project Management Journal (author draft on arXiv, Oxford Said Business School)
claims.quote: Nine out of ten such projects have cost overruns. Overruns of up to 50 percent in real terms are common
claims.use_in_story: Run ten project bars and show nine ending over budget, as the reason early warning on site delays matters.

gaps: NSC Injury Facts pages returned HTTP 403 to all seven fetches (the fetch tool also refuses web.archive.org copies), so the three NSC figures (per death, per injury, total) are unfetched, marked low, and backed only by search extracts plus two fetched secondary pages.
The session WebSearch budget (200 of 200 calls) ran out part-way through. After that I only fetched URLs I already knew and did not route around the limit. Items below marked 'not found' may exist.
No published Saudi or GCC cost of a work-related fatality was found. The GOSI employer FAQ has no death benefit amounts and the GOSI benefit schedule was not reachable.
No GCC statistics beyond Saudi Arabia were retrieved (no injury rate, construction share or fatality cost for Qatar, UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain or Oman).

GASTAT does not split construction out of its survey wage table that I could reach. The Industry line (which includes mining, manufacturing, utilities and construction) is a proxy, and the Q2 2026 register-based wage by activity table could not be read.

The GOSI 2023 absolute injury count and cause split are unconfirmed. The SPA article body did not load (headline only). The count 27,133 appeared only in search extracts. No GOSI 2024 count was found. GASTAT's 2024 rate is the newest Saudi injury figure here.
No primary or reputable source for labour share of project cost was fetched, so none is included. No Saudi cost-of-delay per day was found either, only the percentage overruns.

McKinsey Global Institute 2017 pages (productivity growth 1% against 2.8% for the world economy; large projects 20% longer and up to 80% over budget) timed out on all seven attempts. The productivity figures were seen only on a secondary wiki page, so I left them out.
The ISSA PDF at issa.int returned HTTP 403, so the number of companies and countries behind the 2.2 ratio is unconfirmed. The DGUV project page was used instead.
The $4 to $6 return appears only as a quote inside an ASSP white paper. The original OSHA Office of Regulatory Analysis document and its year were not found.

ILO share-of-GDP numbers differ: 3.94% (2017), 'around 5 percent' and 'exceeds 4%' (ILO Oct 2025, different pages) and 5.8% (2024 journal). I did not reconcile them. The ILOSTAT 2025 blog returned HTTP 403, and no ILO global death estimate newer than the 2019 year was found.
Latest-year checks are partial: NSC 2024, HSE 2023/24 and GASTAT 2024 may have newer editions that I did not look for. Saudi Gazette (HTTP 402) and Arabian Business (HTTP 403) could not be opened.
Several PDFs (ILO, GASTAT, ASSP, Cureus, arXiv) could not be parsed by the fetch tool. I extracted their text locally with the macOS PDF engine and checked each quote against that text.
